title: Chromosome-level assembly and analysis of three hydroxy fatty acid-producing Physaria species

paper_content.abstract: Several Physaria species (Brassicaceae) produce abundant hydroxy fatty acids in their seeds, with industrial applications. Here, we report three chromosome-level genomes of Physaria species: P. lindheimeri, P. pallida and P. fendleri, with sizes of 344 Mb, 329 Mb and 452 Mb, respectively. Comparative genome analysis reveals that these three Physaria species diverged from Arabidopsis thaliana approximately 14.10-14.46 million years ago and underwent two consecutive Physaria-specific whole-genome duplication events. Their centromeres harbor an 111-bp satellite repeat and two retrotransposon classes (Gypsy/CRM, Copia/Ale). Transcriptomic analysis identifies seed-highly expressed lipid synthesis genes potentially underlying unique fatty acid profiles. Furthermore, we pinpoint the two residues in FAH12 variants that cause the disparity in hydroxylation activity among the three Physaria species. Taken together, this study provides important genomic resources for investigating the evolution of Physaria species and developing industrial oil crops for sustainable production of hydroxy fatty acids.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript reports whole genome sequencing of three related Physaria species which accumulate industrial useful hydroxy fatty acids. Authors made comparative studies and annotated a list of lipid genes among Arabidopsis and the three physaria species. The methods are up-to-date and the work meets the expected standards in genome sequencing field. Authors obtained novel genomic data, and the informative is critical for future understanding the mechanisms underlying HFA biosynthesis.
Specific comments.
1. Regarding the mechanisms of accumulating different levels of HFA among these three Physaria species, Author mainly focused on the FAH12 genes and enzyme activity. It is known that PfFAH12 is a bi-functional hydroxylase/desaturase, and PlFAH12 is a strict FAH12. Authors didn’t mine the data deeply, nor characterize the other important genes such as LPAT2s. 20:1OH may enter the TAGs through Kennedy pathway, it will be valuable if additional in vitro experiments are performed to characterize the substrate specificity on the three LPAT2s (PfLPAT2, PpLPAT2 and PlLPAT2).
2. Nomenclature ‘KCS3’. Arabidopsis lipid genes are routinely used as standards to name orthologous genes. The original ‘KCS3’ for the HFA-specific condensing enzyme from P. fendleri is orthologous to AtKCS18 (or AtFAE1). Since Arabidopsis has AtKCS3 which synthesizes very long fatty acids, it is better to clarify the nature of ‘KCS3’ used in the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The current submitted manuscript by Wang et al titled "Chromosome-level assembly and analysis of three hydroxy fatty acids producing Physaria species: P. lindheimeri, P. pallida and P. fendleri" report the full genome and transcriptome analyses for three Physaria species which showed varying capacity in total seed oil content and hydroxy fatty acid content as well. After comparative transcriptomic analysis, the transcript of the major gene resonponsable for HFA synthesis showed high expression in species that has lower FAH content. Based on this finding, the authors looked into details in FAH12 protein sequence and predicted 3-D structure by alpha-fold. The authors then identfied two amino acid substitutions in this protein, and through some in vitro activity assay, and conclude that the two amino acids changes explain the difference in FAH12 activity then likely the hydroxy fatty acid content. The first genome and transcriptomic part is some-how dis-associated from the second part. The paper is straight forward and well written. The data presented is solide but with a major descriptive part. But I consider that the finding in this paper does not reach the level of Nature Communications. I recommend the authors submit the paper to a more plant-specific journal.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Authors finished chromosome-level assemblies of three plants, including P. lindheimeri, P. pallida and P. fendleri. and then performed comparative genome analyses among them and with other plant genomes. There are several major conclusions that they got. First, three genome reference genomes have been released. Second, they revealed that the three Physaria species diverged from Arabidopsis thaliana approximately 31 14.10-14.46 million years ago and underwent two consecutive Physaria-specific whole-genome duplication events. Third, they presented the evolutionary features of centromere sequences. Forth, they find that duplicated genomic regions are associated with maintenance of species biological homeostasis and adaptation to environmental fluctuations. Fifth, transcriptomic analysis shows gene expression profiles that related to lipid synthesis in the seeds. Last, through wetlab works, they find the two residues in FAH12 that caused the disparity in hydroxylation activity among three Physaria species. This work is fine, however, the genomic analysis part is quite common, and there is no striking finding. The wetlab part only provided indirect evidences to support the conclusion.
Major concerns:
1.I am not sure if it is feasible to assay the activity of FAH12 in the animal cells. Animal cells are not plant cell after all. Instead, author should do the transgenic validation in Physaria. In Fig6a, the content of (C20:1-OH) content is highest in P. pallida, however, in Fig6b, PpFAH12WT show lowest C18:1-OH. Both is not consistent. Additionally, the differences of the content in fig6b among these plants are not obvious.
2. Author did some analysis at the centromere regions. Actually, assembling quality of centromere regions has been validated by any other ways although long reads to be used. Therefore, it is a risk to do any analysis about the centromere region.
Minor concerns:
1. Iine 50 author say” Some Physaria species exhibit valuable traits that are conducive to domestication”. It is not clear if is there any physaria species have been cultivated as crops.
2. Author should introduce the usage of HFA from Physaria species to industry.
3. Author should introduce the physical and chemical properties of HFA from Physaria,
4. The author highlighted the unique, twice-occurring whole genome duplication events in the Physaria genus using Ks plots and genome synteny between P. lindheimeri and A. thaliana. However, the analysis still has several issues that need to be addressed to provide more robust evidence for the conclusions: A 4DTv plot may provide more detailed resolution regarding the WGD events.
5. Figures 2c, 2d, and 2e should use the same Ks color bar and have P. lindheimeri on the Y-axis. Alternatively, creating a Sankey plot including all related species could make the relationships more evident.
6. The author did not clearly explain how new centromeres and telomeres formed during species differentiation, given the extensive chromosome breaks and fusions in the ancient Physaria genus over such a short interval. Generally, new centromere loci have structural or sequence preferences.

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript reports whole genome sequencing of three related Physaria species which accumulate industrial useful hydroxy fatty acids. Authors made comparative studies and annotated a list of lipid genes among Arabidopsis and the three physaria species. The methods are up-to-date and the work meets the expected standards in genome sequencing field. Specific comments.
1. Regarding the mechanisms of accumulating different levels of HFA among these three Physaria species, Author mainly focused on the FAH12 genes and enzyme activity. It is known that PfFAH12 is a bi-functional hydroxylase/desaturase, and PlFAH12 is a strict FAH12. Authors didn’t mine the data deeply, nor characterize the other important genes such as LPAT2s. 20:1OH may enter the TAGs through Kennedy pathway, it will be valuable if additional in vitro experiments are performed to characterize the substrate specificity on the three LPAT2s (PfLPAT2, PpLPAT2 and PlLPAT2).

The original ‘KCS3’ for the HFA-specific condensing enzyme from P. fendleri is orthologous to AtKCS18 (or AtFAE1). ### Reviewer 2

The current submitted manuscript by Wang et al titled "Chromosome-level assembly and analysis of three hydroxy fatty acids producing Physaria species: P. lindheimeri, P. pallida and P. fendleri" report the full genome and transcriptome analyses for three Physaria species which showed varying capacity in total seed oil content and hydroxy fatty acid content as well. Authors finished chromosome-level assemblies of three plants, including P. lindheimeri, P. pallida and P. fendleri. and then performed comparative genome analyses among them and with other plant genomes. ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript reports whole genome sequencing of three related Physaria species which accumulate industrial useful hydroxy fatty acids. Authors made comparative studies and annotated a list of lipid genes among Arabidopsis and the three physaria species. The methods are up-to-date and the work meets the expected standards in genome sequencing field. Authors obtained novel genomic data, and the informative is critical for future understanding the mechanisms underlying HFA biosynthesis.
Specific comments.
1. Regarding the mechanisms of accumulating different levels of HFA among these three Physaria species, Author mainly focused on the FAH12 genes and enzyme activity. It is known that PfFAH12 is a bi-functional hydroxylase/desaturase, and PlFAH12 is a strict FAH12. Authors didn’t mine the data deeply, nor characterize the other important genes such as LPAT2s. 20:1OH may enter the TAGs through Kennedy pathway, it will be valuable if additional in vitro experiments are performed to characterize the substrate specificity on the three LPAT2s (PfLPAT2, PpLPAT2 and PlLPAT2).
2. Nomenclature ‘KCS3’. Arabidopsis lipid genes are routinely used as standards to name orthologous genes. The original ‘KCS3’ for the HFA-specific condensing enzyme from P. fendleri is orthologous to AtKCS18 (or AtFAE1). Since Arabidopsis has AtKCS3 which synthesizes very long fatty acids, it is better to clarify the nature of ‘KCS3’ used in the manuscript.

6. The author did not clearly explain how new centromeres and telomeres formed during
species differentiation, given the extensive chromosome breaks and fusions in the
ancient Physaria genus over such a short interval. Generally, new centromere loci have
structural or sequence preferences.
[Response]: Thanks for your kind suggestion. In the original manuscript we did indeed
provide insufficient detail on the mechanism underlying the rapid formation of new
centromeres and telomeres. However, we identified seven-base telomeric repeats (5'-
TTTAGGG-3') in all three genomes, which are telomere-specific sequences (Fig 1c).
Moreover, we also identified satellite repeat sequence with a length of 111 bp in all
three genomes, which was confirmed in rice, Arabidopsis, and maize (Cheng et al.,
2002; Naish et al., 2021; Wolfgruber et al., 2009). Based on this characteristic, we
identified the centromeric regions of chromosomes in the genomes of P. lindheimeri,
P. pallida, and P. fendleri (Fig. 4a and Fig. S9). In P. lindheimeri genome, centromeres
exhibit a length range of 2.18 Mb to 3.14 Mb, with an average length of 2.62 Mb, and
each centromere contains an average of 4,308 satellite repeat sequences. In P. pallida
genome, centromeres span from 1.52 Mb to 4.96 Mb, with an average length of 3.55
Mb, and each centromere contains an average of 4,664 satellite repeat sequences.
Similarly, in P. fendleri genome, centromere lengths range from 1.48 Mb to 3.26 Mb,
with an average length of 2.36 Mb, and each centromere contains an average of 5,439
satellite repeat sequences. (Table S11). Furthermore, we identified satellite repeat
sequence with a length of 111 bp in all three genomes. It is noteworthy that the satellite
repeat units among the three Physaria species are highly similar. The identity between
the satellite repeat sequences of P. lindheimeri and P. pallida reaches 94%, while the
average sequence identity of centromeric satellite sequences within chromosomes is as
high as 96%. This result suggests the significant conservation of satellite repeat units
in the centromeric regions of these plant genomes.
Within species of the Physaria genus, we identified an enrichment of two classes
of retrotransposons, Gypsy/CRM and Copia/Ale, in the centromeric regions
(Fig. 4a and Fig. S9). Specifically, the copy numbers of Gypsy/CRM type
retrotransposons range from 387 to 577 on each chromosome, while the copy numbers
of Copia/Ale type retrotransposons range from 147 to 297. Despite P. fendleri having
the largest genome among three species, we observed the lowest copy numbers of
Gypsy/CRM and Copia/Ale retrotransposons in its centromeric regions. Subsequently, we
quantified the proportions of several transposons frequently occurring in the genome.
We found that transposons within the centromere region were predominantly composed of
LTR/Gypsy (85%), followed by LTR/Copia (10%). In contrast, non-centromeric
regions exhibited similar proportions of LTR/Gypsy (35%) and LTR/Copia (35%),
indicating distinct transposon distributions between these regions (Response Fig 5).
